results.content: # Nanometer-thick magnet produced at room temperature using lasers could one day produce better HDDs, faster non-silicon processors. * **Laser pulses altered magnet behavior by up to forty percent at room temperature**. Their study, published in *Nature Communications*, explores whether magnetic excitations can be tuned optically in ultrathin materials operating at room temperature and under modest magnetic fields. The direction of the frequency change depended on both the applied magnetic field and the laser fluence. The researchers describe this behavior as on-demand laser-induced frequency tuning of coherent magnons in a nanometer-thick magnet at room temperature. Put simply, the researchers found a way to use brief flashes of light to dial magnetic behavior up or down in a material thinner than a human hair while it operates at room temperature. ***Follow TechRadar on Google News*** and***add us as a preferred source*** *to get our expert news, reviews, and opinion in your feeds.

results.content: # Magnets produced at room temperature using lasers could produce faster non-silicon processors. * **Researchers demonstrate room temperature laser control of magnons in thin magnetic materials**. * **Visible light pulses tune magnetic frequencies without cryogenic conditions**. Researchers have demonstrated a new way to tune magnetic behavior in extremely thin materials using visible laser pulses at room temperature. In this new work, the researchers instead used short visible light laser pulses combined with a modest external magnetic field below 200mT. By adjusting laser intensity and magnetic field strength, the team could reliably choose whether the magnon frequency increased or decreased. The combination of room temperature operation, visible light control, and nanometer scale thickness means this approach could fit into future storage, signal processing, and spin based computing systems. Hard drives and large cloud servers rely on magnetic materials, and being able to control them more precisely with light could allow data to be written and moved much quicker than it is today.
